items.title: Graph-Based Orchestration of Agent Workflows
items.abstract:
Graph-Based Orchestration of Agent Workflows was recorded as a Main Track session at the 2026 AI Engineering Summit. The session focuses on the engineering of reliable agents, tool use, orchestration, and state management. The project referenced by this session is langchain-ai/langgraph. Programme notes describe the project as: A library for building stateful, graph-structured agent workflows with durable execution, cycles, and human-in-the-loop control. The speaker combines architecture diagrams, production anecdotes, and benchmark results, and reserves time at the end for questions from practitioners.

Observability receives a full section. The speaker demonstrates span-level traces that connect a user request to each planning step, tool invocation, retry, and final artifact.

The team presents a checklist for reliability: deterministic tool adapters, idempotent actions, checkpointed state, and replayable transcripts for every long-running task.

Several examples show how to keep an agent grounded in an environment: sandboxed file systems, browser sessions, shell access, and structured observations that the model can verify.

The session compares single-agent loops with multi-agent topologies and argues that most production failures come from unclear handoffs rather than weak models.

The speaker opens with a taxonomy of agent runtimes: planners, executors, tool routers, memory services, and policy layers that decide when an autonomous loop should stop and ask for help.

A recurring theme is that tool interfaces are the real contract. Schemas drift, permissions change, and retries multiply unless every tool call is validated, traced, and bounded by an explicit timeout.

Method and measurement. The speaker explains how they decided which optimizations were worth maintaining and which were removed after the experiment. Failure analysis is given as much time as the success story, including a list of assumptions that did not survive contact with real traffic. The speaker is explicit about the difference between microbenchmarks and end-to-end product measurements. The team used a staged rollout with canary traffic, automatic rollback, and a weekly review of quality regressions.

Takeaways. The final advice is to document the assumptions behind a benchmark, because those assumptions are what future maintainers will question. Questions about scale were answered with a reminder that the operational envelope matters more than the peak headline number. A second takeaway is that observability and evaluation must be designed together with the feature. Attendees should leave with a concrete checklist for reproducing the core result in their own environment.

Session context. Examples were drawn from internal tools, customer-facing assistants, and open-source deployments. The speaker used production incidents as teaching material and was candid about what failed before the final design. The presentation assumes familiarity with Python and basic model-serving concepts but does not require research experience.

The session included a brief discussion of privacy, including how long traces are retained and how user data is scrubbed before storage.

A comparison slide showed the same workload before and after the change, with percentile latencies rather than averages so that tail behavior was visible.

A follow-up workshop covers the hands-on version of the same material, with exercises that rebuild a small end-to-end pipeline.

Several recommendations were framed as defaults that teams can start with and then relax only after measuring the tradeoff in their own environment.

The presenter emphasized that tooling should make the safe path the easy path, because operators under pressure tend to take shortcuts.

During the audience discussion, one participant described a similar rollout that stalled because ownership was split across teams; the speaker recommended a single service owner for the end-to-end workflow.

The talk included a short retrospective on what the team would do differently if they started again with the same constraints.

The speaker drew a distinction between a demo that succeeds once and a system that succeeds repeatedly under noisy inputs.

Audience questions ranged from hardware selection to team structure, and the answers consistently returned to clarity of measurement.

The speaker answered a question about security by describing the permission model, the sandbox boundary, and the review process for sensitive actions.

The presenter noted that documentation quality often determines whether a technique is adopted, since most teams first encounter the idea through an internal write-up rather than the original paper.

items.title: Observability for RAG Pipelines
items.abstract:
Observability for RAG Pipelines was recorded as a Lightning Talk session at the 2026 AI Engineering Summit. The session focuses on developer platforms, observability, and workflow automation around LLM applications. The project referenced by this session is traceloop/openllmetry. Programme notes describe the project as: the open-source openllmetry project, which the speaker uses as the reference implementation for the techniques shown on stage. The speaker combines architecture diagrams, production anecdotes, and benchmark results, and reserves time at the end for questions from practitioners.

The speaker argues that observability must capture structured spans, not just logs, because tool calls and retries are the unit of debugging.

The speaker highlights hidden operational costs: token accounting, noisy alerts, and experiments that never reach a clear conclusion.

The closing discussion focuses on developer experience for non-specialists who build with natural-language interfaces.

The session surveys the toolchain around modern model applications: tracing, prompt management, evals, deployment, and incident response.

Compiler and runtime approaches are compared for graph-structured applications, including scheduling, caching, and partial re-execution.

Prompt versioning is treated like code versioning, with review, rollback, and environment promotion rules that prevent accidental regressions.

Method and measurement. Each experiment reports hardware, batch sizes, prompt templates, and evaluation settings so the audience can judge how far the result will transfer. The speaker explains how they decided which optimizations were worth maintaining and which were removed after the experiment. A cost table compares tokens, latency, engineering hours, and operational risk for each option discussed. Failure analysis is given as much time as the success story, including a list of assumptions that did not survive contact with real traffic.

Takeaways. The team encourages readers to treat every generated artifact as untrusted until verified by a deterministic check. The final advice is to document the assumptions behind a benchmark, because those assumptions are what future maintainers will question. The main takeaway is to measure the bottleneck before redesigning the architecture. The speaker recommends starting with the simplest configuration that satisfies the product requirement.

Session context. The speaker contrasted research prototypes with systems that must run unattended overnight and recover from partial failures. The speaker used production incidents as teaching material and was candid about what failed before the final design. Several audience members asked for reproducible configurations, and the speaker pointed to the referenced project as the starting point.

items.abstract:

The speaker combines architecture diagrams, production anecdotes, and benchmark results, and reserves time at the end for questions from practitioners.

The talk examines contamination, leakage, and benchmark saturation, with practical tests for detecting them before leaders rely on a score.

Safety filters are evaluated on both false positives and false negatives, because over-blocking quietly destroys user trust and product metrics.

The closing segment connects evaluation results to release decisions and rollback criteria.

The speaker argues for reproducible evaluation artifacts: frozen datasets, versioned prompts, and recorded model snapshots.

Red-teaming is presented as a continuous program with ownership, triage, and regression tests rather than a one-off exercise.

Benchmark construction is described step by step: task sampling, rubric design, annotator agreement, and adversarial case mining.

items.title: Distilling Frontier Models into Small Ones
